title: An operational defense against civilization-threatening asteroid impacts

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an operational system that can discover a potentially civilization-threatening asteroid, determine whether it will strike Earth, assess its physical properties, organize a timely response, and verify that a deflection has removed the collision threat. Its defining advance would be the dependable integration of detection, orbit determination, characterization, decision-making, launch readiness and measured trajectory change. This is a proposed capability; the supplied evidence establishes important components but does not establish the operational completeness of the entire system.

A demonstrated physical approach is kinetic deflection: a spacecraft strikes an asteroid to change its motion. With an appropriately sized spacecraft and sufficient warning—typically many years to decades in the DART report's explanation—a small orbital change can accumulate into enough separation to avoid a future Earth collision. An operational defense would have to connect that mechanism to a particular threat's trajectory, properties and available response time, then measure whether the intervention actually achieved the required outcome.

significance.text: The revolutionary consequence would be to make some civilization-threatening natural catastrophes preventable through deliberate intervention. Early discovery and effective trajectory alteration could turn an otherwise unavoidable collision into an event that misses Earth. This is a conditional impact judgment grounded in the documented deflection mechanism, rather than evidence that such protection has already been deployed.

Protection would have explicit boundaries. DART demonstrated a response for one asteroid with particular physical properties, and its report emphasizes that one impact is only one data point. Success on that target does not establish effectiveness against much larger bodies, different structures or objects discovered shortly before a possible collision. Discovery coverage and warning time are therefore part of the protective capability itself: a successful impactor cannot protect against a threat that is detected too late for the available response.

Conditional synthesis: a dependable defense could also make assessments of asteroid risk more actionable by linking a predicted collision to a tested response and a quantified residual risk. That possibility depends on reliable institutions and operational readiness as well as spacecraft performance. The useful analogy is a bounded prevention capability for specified hazards; it should not be interpreted as a universal shield against every impactor.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability sought here is dependable performance across the entire defense chain. Detection must occur early enough, orbit estimates must resolve whether intervention is necessary, characterization must support a credible deflection plan, and decisions and mission preparation must fit within the remaining warning time. These are requirements of the proposed system. The supplied historical demonstration and partial budget evidence do not establish whether that complete capability was present or absent as of 1 November 2026.

A major scientific barrier is justified extrapolation from a measured impact to other threat scenarios. The response of a much larger asteroid, or one with different structure and material properties, cannot be assumed from Dimorphos alone. A credible defense needs measurements and validated models that connect the selected intervention to the resulting trajectory change, with uncertainty carried through to the predicted Earth encounter. Its claimed protection must remain limited where that extrapolation has not been demonstrated.

Response readiness is a separate engineering and organizational barrier. The DART report observes that a spacecraft addressing an imminent impact might need to be built much faster than DART, creating programmatic challenges beyond its technology demonstration. An operational system would therefore need credible arrangements for mission preparation, launch, navigation and contingencies under time pressure, alongside the ability to determine whether the completed intervention was sufficient.

Proposed scope clarification: the title's civilization-threatening category needs an explicit scenario definition. Object size alone is insufficient as a test specification; the intended coverage should identify masses, structures, encounter conditions and warning times, and explain why the selected scenarios represent threats at that scale. Without that definition, a demonstration relevant to a major terrestrial hazard could still fall short of validating the scope claimed by this concept.

current_state.text: DART struck Dimorphos on 26 September 2022. Its October 2023 final technical report gives a refined orbital-period change of −33.24 minutes ± 1.4 seconds, meaning that Dimorphos's orbital period around its binary companion was reduced. This is a measured demonstration of kinetic deflection for one target. It was not a demonstration of changing an Earth-bound asteroid onto an Earth-missing trajectory, and it does not by itself establish protection against civilization-threatening impacts.

The report contains an apparent internal numerical inconsistency: section 3.1.3 gives −32.25 minutes for one model, while the supplied review finds that the accompanying post-impact periods are consistent with approximately −33.24 minutes. The executive summary explicitly reports −33.24 minutes ± 1.4 seconds, which is the value retained here. The inconsistency warrants qualification but does not, on the supplied evidence, overturn the demonstrated period reduction.

DART also supplies a concrete precedent for mission rehearsal. Its operations work included closed-loop simulations of nominal and faulted terminal phases, testing of 21 terminal-phase contingencies, real-time practice and simulation of the final 24 hours before the terminal phase. These achievements support confidence in the preparation of that mission. They do not constitute independent exercises of an entire planetary-defense system from discovery through public decisions, rapid launch and verification of an avoided Earth collision.

NASA's FY 2027 budget request lists Near Earth Objects Surveyor as a development project. The earlier research attributes to this budget a five-year objective to discover at least two-thirds of the then-undetected near-Earth objects larger than 140 meters. However, the retained budget text ends before the relevant project description, so the supplied review could verify the development listing but could not verify that numerical objective. The five-year, two-thirds and greater-than-140-meter figures therefore remain an unconfirmed attribution in this record, rather than an established survey result or a disproved claim. Even if confirmed as an objective, they would describe discovery coverage, not demonstrated deflection or civilization-scale protection.

The evidence has specific access limits. According to the supplied review and source index, both retained PDF extractions are partial and report pages without extractable text. Relevant DART passages are readable, although the retained text is truncated in the references; the budget extraction stops before the NEO Surveyor project pages. The budget's April 2026 publication date is supplied metadata rather than a date confirmed in the reviewed content. No bounded freshness-search entries were supplied, so developments and overall operational status through 1 November 2026 remain unverified. These limits constrain the conclusions available here without showing that unverified claims are false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed criterion: publish the threat scenarios the system is intended to address and the limits of its protection. These should connect the civilization-threatening scope to specified object sizes, masses, structures, encounter conditions and warning times. Survey performance should be described with coverage and discovery limitations, while response performance should state the time and physical conditions required for a credible intervention. These are proposed evaluation requirements, not established standards supplied by the sources.
completion_criteria.label: Publish defined threat scenarios and limits of asteroid protection

completion_criteria.text: Proposed criterion: demonstrate a planned, precisely measured deflection of a representative nonhazardous object, with sufficient pre-intervention and post-intervention orbit characterization to test the predicted outcome. DART provides a precedent for measurable deflection and orbit characterization. The proposed extension is to validate how the demonstration supports the defined civilization-threatening scenarios, rather than treating a single successful strike as sufficient evidence for every size or structure.
completion_criteria.label: Measured deflection validates applicability to defined civilization-threatening asteroid scenarios

completion_criteria.text: Proposed criterion: conduct independent end-to-end exercises spanning detection, orbit uncertainty, characterization, decisions, launch readiness, alternative object properties and verification that the resulting trajectory misses Earth. Exercises should include credible faults and timing constraints. DART's rehearsals establish a mission-level precedent for contingency testing; independent assessment of the full defense chain is an additional proposal here.
completion_criteria.label: Independent end-to-end defense exercises verify Earth misses under credible faults

completion_criteria.text: Proposed criterion: make observations, uncertainty estimates, model assumptions and exercise methods sufficiently available for independent analysis and reproduction of the main conclusions. Demonstrations and simulations should establish where predictions remain reliable and where additional evidence is needed, especially when extending results to larger or differently structured objects. A finite program can demonstrate breadth across defined conditions; it cannot establish literal universality. Practical completion would mean a reproducible, bounded claim of protection supported by readiness evidence, with residual gaps stated explicitly.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible protection claims establish predictive limits and state residual gaps

related_concepts.text: Conceptual comparison with the supplied roster: AER-01, Mass-access orbital transportation, overlaps through launch availability and the ability to deliver a response spacecraft on time. Its defining goal is broad access to orbit, whereas AER-07 requires successful intervention against specified impact threats. AER-03, Industrial production of spacecraft propellant from extraterrestrial resources, could conditionally support future response logistics, but the supplied evidence does not establish it as a prerequisite for planetary defense.

Conceptual comparison: AER-02, A probe that returns data from another star system, shares demanding spacecraft navigation, autonomy and remote operations, but addresses interstellar exploration rather than a timely intervention near Earth. AER-08, A space observatory that can test for life on Earth-like exoplanets, overlaps at the broad level of space-based observation; its targets and measurement goals differ from discovering impactors and determining their trajectories.

Conceptual comparison: AER-06, General-purpose robotic construction of very large space systems, could conditionally expand future space infrastructure, but construction capability alone does not establish asteroid detection or deflection performance. AER-05, Economically competitive space-to-Earth solar power, also concerns space infrastructure, with completion governed by useful energy delivery and economics rather than impact prevention. AER-04, Multi-year, near-closed human life support for deep space, concerns sustained human habitation; the supplied planetary-defense concept does not require a crewed intervention.

Conceptual comparison: AER-09, Sustained, useful air-breathing hypersonic flight, and AER-10, Fossil-fuel-free electric propulsion for large, long-range passenger aircraft, share the broad aerospace domain with AER-07. Their central challenges concern atmospheric flight and aircraft propulsion, respectively. Neither establishes the survey, orbital assessment, spacecraft response or verified deflection capabilities that define this entry.

brief.title: A working defense against catastrophic asteroid impacts
possible: People could prevent an asteroid collision that would threaten civilization. A working defense would find the object early, establish whether it will hit Earth, assess its properties, organize a response and confirm that the changed path safely misses Earth.
One approach would send a spacecraft to strike the asteroid. With enough warning, a small change in its motion could grow into enough separation to avoid a collision.
why: Some natural catastrophes that threaten civilization could become preventable. Governments could connect a predicted collision to a tested response, with a measured estimate of the danger remaining afterward.

sources.who: Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory and collaborators
sources.showed: The DART spacecraft struck Dimorphos and shortened its circuit around its companion asteroid. The mission also rehearsed failures during the final approach.
sources.quote: Within 2 weeks of impact, it was clear that the orbit of Dimorphos had been significantly altered.
sources.cited_for: A spacecraft strike can measurably change an asteroid's motion.
sources.not_established: The mission did not demonstrate an avoided Earth collision or dependable protection against larger or differently structured asteroids.

sources.showed: NASA's budget request lists Near Earth Objects Surveyor as a development project.
sources.cited_for: Asteroid discovery is part of NASA's planned planetary defense work.
sources.not_established: A development project does not establish achieved discovery coverage or an ability to prevent an impact.

shown: NASA's DART mission, developed and operated by Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory, shortened Dimorphos's circuit around its companion asteroid by about 33 minutes. This demonstrated a change in motion on a single target.
missing: The complete chain needs a demonstration linking early discovery, collision prediction, asteroid assessment, decisions, launch and confirmed avoidance.
Measurements and tested predictions must establish how a strike would affect much larger asteroids and those with different structures.
Mission preparation, launch and backup plans need to work within the warning time available for a real threat.

milestones.label: The threats and protection limits are published
milestones.explanation: Published scenarios would have to specify asteroid size, mass, structure, approach and warning time, alongside discovery and response limits. These would define which civilization-threatening impacts the defense must handle.

milestones.label: A measured deflection supports the defined threat scenarios
milestones.explanation: A planned strike on a harmless asteroid would need precise path measurements before and afterward to test predictions. The result would have to validate its relevance to the defined civilization-threatening scenarios.

milestones.label: Independent exercises confirm avoidance despite credible failures
milestones.explanation: Independent exercises would have to cover discovery through confirmed avoidance, including uncertain paths, different asteroid properties, decisions, launch readiness, faults and deadlines. This would test the complete defense chain.

milestones.label: Others can reproduce protection claims and their limits
milestones.explanation: Independent analysts would need observations, uncertainty estimates, assumptions and exercise methods to reproduce the conclusions. Together with readiness evidence, these would establish reliable predictions and remaining gaps.

uncertain: The asteroid scenarios that count as civilization-threatening, and suitable demonstration targets, remain undefined.
Acceptable remaining collision risk, required warning times and readiness thresholds still need to be specified.

page.title: Planetary defense against globally destructive asteroid impacts
page.definition: A planetary defense system that discovers and tracks an asteroid on a collision course with Earth, measures its physical properties, and verifies that a deflection makes it miss Earth. The scope is an impact capable of worldwide damage. The National Research Council places that possibility above roughly 2–3 km in diameter, with an uncertain lower limit. In a flight test, DART struck Dimorphos and changed both its orbit around Didymos and the pair’s orbit around the Sun.

goal.need: An asteroid roughly 1 km across could kill many millions of people and disrupt the climate enough to cause years of crop failures worldwide. Surveys have found more than 96% of the estimated near-Earth objects at least 1 km across. Tracking gives advance warning. Deflecting an asteroid would prevent the collision and spare harvests far beyond the impact site. Doing so by spacecraft impact requires a spacecraft large enough for the target and typically many years to decades of warning.

completion.title: An asteroid capable of worldwide damage is diverted from a confirmed Earth-impact trajectory.
completion.criterion: For one asteroid whose pre-intervention observations establish an Earth-impact trajectory and whose assessed impact effects include worldwide damage, complete discovery, orbit determination, physical characterization, response authorization, launch and deflection. Post-intervention tracking must establish that the changed orbit misses Earth at the threatened encounter, with orbital uncertainty propagated; that encounter must subsequently occur without collision. Record diameter, mass, encounter geometry and warning time. The claim covers that encounter.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas fallback; no external integrated completion test was located.
completion.basis: Searches of NASA’s 2023 strategy, the 2010 and 2023 National Academies reports, NITEP’s 2021 protocols and IAWN/SMPAG’s 2025 report located component requirements and response triggers, but no integrated acceptance test or accepted residual-risk ceiling for this capability. This fallback requires an actual prevented impact in one specified worldwide-damage scenario.

milestones.title: DART changes Dimorphos’s orbital period around Didymos by at least 73 seconds.
milestones.criterion: Change Dimorphos’s orbital period around Didymos by at least 73 seconds through spacecraft impact. Measure the period change from ground-based observations before and after impact with uncertainty no greater than 7.3 seconds at one standard deviation.
milestones.set_by: NASA, DART Level 1 requirements DART-2 and DART-3, reproduced in the final technical report. These requirements were written specifically for Dimorphos.
milestones.threshold_quote: shall cause at least a 73-s change in the binary orbital period.

milestones.title: A catalogue contains at least 90% of near-Earth objects at least 140 metres in diameter.
milestones.criterion: Detect, track, catalogue and physically characterize near-Earth objects at least 140 m in diameter. Catalogue completeness is measured against the statistically predicted population in that size range. The Act set a goal of 90% completeness within 15 years of its enactment on 30 December 2005.
milestones.set_by: United States Congress, George E. Brown, Jr. Near-Earth Object Survey Act, Public Law 109–155, section 321(d)(1).

milestones.title: Dimorphos’s mass is measured with a relative error of at most 10%.
milestones.criterion: Determine the mass of Dimorphos with a relative error of at most 10%. Hera lists 1% relative error as a separate goal.
milestones.set_by: European Space Agency, Hera Mission Requirements Document, issue 2.10, section 4.1, objective D1. This requirement was written specifically for Dimorphos.

milestones.title: A rapid-response flyby characterizes a near-Earth object approximately 50–100 metres across.
milestones.criterion: Complete a rapid-response flyby reconnaissance demonstration at a near-Earth object approximately 50–100 m in diameter, representative of the population specified by the decadal survey, and assess the capabilities and limitations of flyby characterization. The recommendation specifies no numerical response-time limit.
milestones.set_by: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, Origins, Worlds, and Life, Chapter 18 recommendation on the demonstration mission following DART and NEO Surveyor.
milestones.threshold_quote: a rapid-response, flyby reconnaissance mission targeted to a challenging NEO, representative of the population (~50–100 m in diameter)

milestones.title: A flight exercise completes the defense chain and verifies a miss in its simulated Earth encounter.
milestones.criterion: Complete an integrated flight exercise covering discovery, orbit determination, physical characterization, response decisions, launch, physical deflection and orbit verification within the scenario’s declared warning time. Use a non-threatening asteroid. Propagate the measured deflection and orbital uncertainty to the simulated Earth encounter and verify that the intervention changes the outcome from collision to miss.
milestones.set_by: Technology Atlas fallback. Searches of NASA’s 2023 strategy, NITEP’s 2021 protocols and the 2023 National Academies decadal survey located exercise objectives but no integrated flight-exercise success criterion.

milestones.title: A laboratory impact measures momentum transfer to an asteroid analogue.
milestones.criterion: Measure the target’s change in momentum after an impact on asteroid-like material and report its ratio to the incident projectile momentum. This ratio is the momentum enhancement factor, β.
milestones.set_by: Laboratory asteroid-impact experiments use the momentum enhancement factor to quantify transfer, as defined and measured by Durda and colleagues.
milestones.threshold_quote: The ratio of the momentum change of the target to the impact momentum

milestones.title: Surveys discover 90% of near-Earth objects larger than 1 km.
milestones.criterion: Discover 90% of the estimated population of near-Earth objects larger than 1 km. The Spaceguard programme set a ten-year target, from 1998 to 2008.
milestones.set_by: NASA Near Earth Object Observations Program, Spaceguard survey objective presented to the United Nations Scientific and Technical Subcommittee.
milestones.threshold_quote: Discover 90% of NEOs larger than 1 kilometer in size within 10 years (1998 – 2008)

milestones.title: An impact changes a near-Earth asteroid’s heliocentric semimajor axis by over 100 m, measured to 1%.
milestones.criterion: Use a spacecraft impact to change the semimajor axis of a near-Earth asteroid’s orbit around the Sun by more than 100 m in magnitude. Measure that change to 1% accuracy. The percentage applies to the change in semimajor axis.
milestones.set_by: European Space Agency, orbital-change objective for the Don Quijote Phase A studies, reproduced by the QinetiQ-led study team.
milestones.threshold_quote: Change the asteroid’s semi-major axis by > 100 m and measure the change to 1% accuracy.

results.finding: Dimorphos’s orbital period around Didymos shortened by 33.24 minutes after one DART impact.
results.detail: The two ground-based photometric analyses independently met the precision requirement. The executive summary gives the refined 1.4-second uncertainty.
results.quote: a –33.24 min ± 1.4 s orbital period change

results.finding: LICIACube returned 426 scientific images from its flyby of Dimorphos, its one flyby target.
results.detail: LICIACube imaged the system immediately before and after the impact, with closest approach approximately 58 km from Dimorphos.
results.quote:
In total, 426 scientific images were returned, and LICIACube continued to communicate 
with Earth for ~1 month following its Didymos flyby, after which time communication was lost.

results.finding: DART’s kinetic deflection test shortened the binary orbital period of its one target, Dimorphos, by 33.24 minutes.
results.detail: The project selected an already known binary system for a planned flight test. The verified orbit change concerned Dimorphos’s motion around Didymos.
results.quote: a –33.24 min ± 1.4 s orbital period change

results.finding: Dimorphos’s post-DART orbital period around Didymos was 11.3667 hr in a preliminary fit to three nights of Gemini North observations.
results.detail: The fit assumes a constant period since 2022/2023. The observations leave open whether the period evolved after impact.
results.quote: This yields a binary orbital period of 11.3667 +/- 0.0002 hr (3-sigma), assuming that the period has been constant since 2022/2023.

results.finding: Dimorphos (one asteroid): the mass estimate has about 15% relative uncertainty at 1σ.
Didymos (one binary asteroid system): DART reduced the heliocentric semimajor axis by 360 m.
results.quote: a −360 ± 40m change in the semimajor axis of the system’s orbit around the Sun

results.finding: Near-Earth asteroids larger than 1 km were about 93% discovered, based on 428 NEOWISE survey detections.
results.detail: The supplied text is an accepted arXiv manuscript that acknowledges referee review. The discovery percentage is calculated from the reported counts.
results.quote: of identifying 90% of all NEAs larger than 1 km has been met and exceeded.

results.finding: Dimorphos’s inferred pre-impact mass from 32 listed converged simulations has a conditional upper uncertainty of 11.3% relative to the nominal mean.
results.detail: The mass interval is calculated from the reported density interval using the fixed volume in Eq. S18. The approximately 1% mass residual is the model’s iteration convergence tolerance.
results.quote:
Propagating the 
published 1σ uncertainty of 0.10 mm s⁻¹ in ΔvT  (2), while holding the remaining ejecta parameters 
fixed and with equal weighting of the accepted solutions, gives a conditional central 68.3% interval 
of 1297.84–1597.73 kg m⁻³ for the momentum-inferred density.

results.finding: Hayabusa2 flyby reconnaissance of one asteroid, Torifune, estimated its average diameter at 540 m.
results.detail: JAXA reports size and orbit estimates and notes that further analysis may revise the shape model and size or yield additional physical properties.
results.quote: Torifune is estimated to have a major axis of approximately 840 m, a minor axis of approximately 340 m, and an average diameter of 540 m.

results.finding: For Apophis (one asteroid), the campaign’s estimated impact probability peaked at 16% before radar astrometry ruled out impact.
results.detail: The hypothetical impact trajectory was held fixed while its uncertainty was updated. The observed trajectory’s estimated risk fell as new measurements constrained the orbit.
results.quote:
The peak (16%) was reached on 2021
February 16, when the ζ uncertainty was 27,000 km.
